# Anthropic files to go public as AI spending outgrows cash

The bills for AI computing power now outrun what even large builders earn. On Monday, Anthropic filed to sell shares to the public, Meta began its first share sale since it went public, and SpaceX agreed to rent its next chips rather than buy them. UBIK slightly favours Anthropic's shares trading before Thanksgiving.

The same AI demand pushes up memory-chip prices. That made South Korea's national income jump while its households spent less. German factories pay more for those parts, and more of them run short, so UBIK expects their recovery to come later and cost more.

Nigeria's only Ebola patient has left the country as Congo's epidemic grows, and UBIK expects the US to keep Nigeria and Kenya off its travel ban. Apple admitted a screen fault in its folding iPhone but has few spare phones.

## Meta and SpaceX join Anthropic in raising money for AI

Until now, Anthropic paid for its growth with private money. It raised about $141 billion, most recently $65 billion in May at a value of $965 billion. On Oct. 26 it filed publicly to list its shares on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead about two dozen banks. The filing leaves the share count and the price range blank. The raise could reach $100 billion at a value of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, but that target is reported, not filed. Either end would make it the largest listing on record.

[Will Anthropic's shares start trading before Thanksgiving?](/forecasts/q_20261027_04)

## South Korea's chip boom lifts growth but not household spending

On Oct. 27 the Bank of Korea said the economy grew 1.0% in the third quarter from the second. The bank's August forecast was 0.3%. Chips did most of the work. Exports rose 2.3%, led by semiconductors. Investment in equipment, mostly machines that make chips, rose 4.1%. Manufacturing grew 2.0%, but services grew only 0.2%. Even with a flat fourth quarter, growth for the year comes to about 3.6%, above the bank's 3.3% forecast. The bank publishes a new forecast on Nov. 26.

[Will Germany's imported chips and electronic parts get dearer even faster?](/forecasts/q_20261027_01)

## German business mood rises, but factories run short of parts

On Oct. 26 Ifo said its business climate index rose to 90.2 in October from 89.9. It was the sixth rise in a row and the highest level since spring 2023. The Ifo index fell to 84.4 in April, after the Middle East war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and drove up energy prices. It now stands above its pre-war level of 88.4. All of the October gain came from expectations for the next six months. Firms rated their current business lower, at 88.8 from 89.5. Ifo President Clemens Fuest said: "The economic recovery is continuing." The government and the IMF now expect 1.3% growth this year, after 0.2% in 2025.

[Will more German factories be short of parts in October?](/forecasts/q_20261027_02)

## Nigeria's only Ebola patient leaves as Congo's epidemic grows

On Oct. 20 Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case since 2014. The patient is a 42-year-old Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat in Abuja, who arrived from Uganda. A private hospital treated her for malaria for about nine days before a test found the Bundibugyo strain. On Oct. 26 a Swiss air ambulance flew her to Geneva University Hospital, where she is stable. Her husband is in isolation in Zurich and has no symptoms. Mohamed Janabi, the WHO's director for Africa, said Nigeria now has no Ebola cases. About 52 contacts, mostly health workers who treated her without Ebola protection, stay under watch. The earliest of them reach day 21 around Nov. 10.

[Will America keep Nigeria and Kenya off its Ebola travel ban?](/forecasts/q_20261027_03)

## Apple admits iPhone Duo screen fault but has few spares

Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo, its new folding phone, went on sale on Oct. 23. Within days, owners in at least nine countries posted reports of cracks along the crease, white patches and phantom touches. Until Oct. 26 those reports had no answer from Apple. That day Apple made its first formal statement: "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units." It told owners to contact AppleCare for a free replacement, with or without the paid AppleCare+ plan. It gave no count and no cause.

[Will Apple go two more weeks without promising free Duo screen repairs?](/forecasts/q_20261026_02)

[Will an iPhone Duo ordered on Black Friday still miss Christmas?](/forecasts/q_20261024_03)

forecasts.claim: Will Anthropic's shares start trading before Thanksgiving?
forecasts.resolution_source: Nasdaq trading records and Anthropic's pricing announcement or final prospectus (SEC Rule 424(b) filing), as reported by Reuters, Bloomberg, AP or CNBC
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if Anthropic's common stock (expected ticker ANT, though a different ticker or share class still counts) begins regular trading on the Nasdaq, or on any other U.S. national securities exchange, on or before Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026 (U.S. Eastern time). The date of the first regular trading session decides; a later halt, delisting or withdrawal does not undo it. Pricing the offering does not count unless regular trading also starts by then. When-issued, pre-IPO, private secondary or tokenized trading does not count. No if regular trading has not begun by the end of Nov. 25, 2026, for any reason, including a postponement or withdrawal of the offering; a postponement still counts as Yes if trading nonetheless begins by Nov. 25. Reports published through Nov. 28, 2026 count toward showing when trading began; if none of the named outlets or Nasdaq records show trading beginning by Nov. 25 by then, the answer is No. The offering's size, price, valuation and first-day performance do not affect resolution.

forecasts.claim: Will Germany's imported chips and electronic parts get dearer even faster?
forecasts.resolution_source: Destatis (Federal Statistical Office) press release on import prices for September 2026 (Außenhandelspreise / Importpreise im September 2026), with GENESIS-Online table 61411-0006, product GP09-261 (electronic components), as a fallback.
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if the first-published year-on-year change in the German import price index for electronic components (elektronische Bauelemente) for September 2026 is greater than +16.1%, the figure Destatis published for August 2026. No if it is +16.1% or lower. If the press release does not give the electronic-components figure, compute it from the GENESIS index values for GP09-261 as first published on or before 2026-10-30, September 2026 against September 2025, rounded to one decimal. Later revisions are ignored. Void if by 2026-10-30 Destatis has not published September 2026 import prices, or neither the press release nor GENESIS gives the figure.

forecasts.claim: Will more German factories be short of parts in October?
forecasts.resolution_source: Ifo Institute monthly release on material shortages in German manufacturing (ifo.de), covering its October 2026 survey, or German press reports of that release.
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if the share of manufacturing firms reporting shortages of materials or intermediate products in Ifo's October 2026 survey, as first published by Ifo, is higher than the September 2026 share of 14.6% (or higher than the September figure stated in the October release, if Ifo revises it). No if it is equal or lower. Later revisions to the October figure do not count. Sector figures do not count; only the all-manufacturing share. Where press reports differ from Ifo, Ifo's figure counts. Void if Ifo has not published the October figure by 19 November 2026.

forecasts.claim: Will America keep Nigeria and Kenya off its Ebola travel ban?
forecasts.resolution_source: CDC Port Health legal authorities page for the order suspending entry from countries where Ebola exists (cdc.gov/port-health/legal-authorities/evdorder.html), the CDC's Oct. 22, 2026 boarding declaration order, and any related Federal Register notices
forecasts.resolution_rule: No if any CDC Ebola order signed from Oct. 27 to Nov. 12, 2026 bars entry to the US, or boarding of a US-bound flight, for presence in Nigeria or Kenya in the prior 21 days. This covers adding either country to the entry suspension order (when renewed, amended or let lapse at its Nov. 10 expiry), to the Oct. 22 boarding declaration order, or to any new or replacement order. It counts even if it takes effect after Nov. 12 or is withdrawn later. Yes otherwise. This includes the case where the CDC page and the Federal Register, as published by Nov. 17, 2026, show no such order. State Department advisory levels, CDC travel health notices, entry limits based on nationality and not tied to Ebola, and screening or airport routing that does not bar entry or boarding do not count.

forecasts.claim: Will Apple go two more weeks without promising free Duo screen repairs?
forecasts.resolution_source: Apple's service programs page (support.apple.com/service-programs) and Apple Newsroom; Apple statements and executive remarks, including the Nov. 2, 2026 earnings call, as reported by Reuters, Bloomberg, MacRumors, AppleInsider or 9to5Mac.
forecasts.resolution_rule: Window: Oct. 26 through Nov. 9, 2026, US Pacific time. Yes if in that window Apple makes no public commitment to repair or replace, at no charge, the iPhone Duo's inner display or hinge for affected owners generally in at least one country. No if in the window Apple publishes a service program under which Duo inner displays or hinges are repaired or replaced at no charge; announces coverage beyond its standard one-year warranty, or regardless of accidental damage, under which cracked or failed Duo inner displays or hinges are repaired or replaced at no charge; announces a recall of the Duo; or an Apple executive states such a policy on the record, including on the Nov. 2 earnings call. A regulator's announcement counts only if it states Apple has agreed to such free repairs. A commitment made in the window counts even if it takes effect later or is later narrowed or withdrawn. These do not count: free replacements given case by case under Apple's standard one-year warranty or at store or carrier discretion; statements that Apple is investigating or that cases are rare; edits to troubleshooting guides; software updates; a paid or discounted repair program or a lower paid repair price; a pause or delay in sales without a free-repair commitment. An announcement dated within the window counts if reported by Nov. 12, 2026. If none is reported by Nov. 12, the answer is Yes.

forecasts.claim: Will an iPhone Duo ordered on Black Friday still miss Christmas?
forecasts.resolution_source: Apple's US online store (apple.com) estimated delivery dates for new iPhone Duo orders, as shown on Friday, Nov. 27, 2026. Evidence is a capture of the store page showing those estimates (for example the Internet Archive) or a report by MacRumors, 9to5Mac, AppleInsider or Bloomberg describing them, published by Nov. 30, 2026.
forecasts.resolution_rule: No if, at any time on Nov. 27, 2026 (US Pacific time), Apple's US online store shows an estimated home-delivery date on or before Dec. 25, 2026 for any iPhone Duo configuration (any storage size, colour, unlocked or carrier model). Otherwise Yes if every configuration it offers shows Dec. 26, 2026 or later, or cannot be ordered online (sold out, unavailable or sales halted), including when no configuration can be ordered at all. Where a date range is shown, its earliest date counts; a ship date counts as the delivery date, and a wait such as '4-5 weeks' is counted from Nov. 27. Use the default US estimate shown without a ZIP code, or the estimate for ZIP 10001 if a ZIP is required. Not counted: in-store pickup, walk-in stock, carriers' and other retailers' own channels, and changes to existing orders. A report that gives the store's estimate without naming configurations is read as covering all of them. If no capture or report published by Nov. 30 shows the estimates on Nov. 27, the latest one from Nov. 26 decides, else the earliest from Nov. 28; if there is none from those three days, the answer is No.
